steps.title: Listen to four ways of disagreeing politely.
steps.sub: None of them is rude. Notice how each one begins.

items.text: I’m sorry, but I don’t really agree.
Yeah, but I don’t think that’s true.
I take your point, but I’m not sure about that.

steps.title: Now listen to five turns from a discussion.
steps.sub: Some agree, some disagree, one gives an opinion.

items.text: You know, I think this is probably true.
I’m afraid I don’t really agree.
In my opinion, young people find it very hard to be alone.

steps.title: Look at the four ways of disagreeing again.
steps.sub: Yeah, but … · I take your point, but … · True, but …
steps.prompt: What do all four have in common?
options: They agree with something first, then disagree.
They all begin with a plain no, then explain.
They are all questions rather than statements.
steps.answer: They agree with something first, then disagree.
steps.why: In English you almost always give a small agreement before you disagree. Starting with a flat no sounds aggressive.

steps.title: Giving an opinion, agreeing and disagreeing
steps.html:
What you are doingWhat you say
giving your opinionIn my opinion, … / Personally, I think … / I’d say …
agreeingThat’s a good point. / I think you’ve got a point. / Yeah, I agree.
disagreeing politelyI’m afraid I disagree. / I’m sorry, but I don’t really agree.
half-agreeingI take your point, but … / True, but there are other ways to look at it.
no strong viewI’m not sure about that. / I don’t have strong views on this.
asking for an opinionWhat do you think? / Do you agree?

In my opinion is followed by a clause, not by to: In my opinion, people share too much, not In my opinion to share.

I’m afraid I disagree is polite, not weak. I’m afraid is the standard softener, as it was at the hotel and in the restaurant.

The pattern agree a little + but is the safest way to disagree with a stranger: True, but …

Careful: the verb is agree, not be agree. Say I agree, never I am agree.

You will use the same phrases in Unit 12 when you answer interview questions.

steps.title: Short presentation · model
steps.html:
A three-minute talk on the same question. You will plan your own at the end.

Is privacy dead?

Is privacy dead? · a three-minute talk

Introduction. Good morning. Today I’m going to talk about privacy, and about one question: do we still have any? I’ll look at three things — what has changed, what we have gained, and what I think we should do.

Firstly, what has changed. People used to share their news with ten or twenty people. Now a photograph can reach three million in an evening. A man in New York invited fifteen guests to dinner; the guests posted photos, and over three million people saw his dinner party.

In addition, we give this information away ourselves. Nobody makes us do it. In my opinion, that is the real change: not cameras in the street, but the phone in our own hand.

On the other hand, there are real benefits. Being online helps people find work, keep in touch with family abroad and get help quickly.

To sum up, privacy is not dead, but it is now something you have to choose. If we understood how much we give away, I think we would give away less. Thank you — are there any questions?

steps.title: Plan a three-minute talk on a question you care about.
steps.sub: About 150–200 words. Follow the five parts of the model.
steps.placeholder: Good morning. Today I’m going to talk about …
steps.html:
1. Plan (from the model): introduction and what you will cover → first point → second point with your own opinion → the other side → conclusion and an invitation for questions.
  • Good morning. Today I’m going to talk about … I’ll look at three things: …
  • Firstly, …
  • In addition, … In my opinion, …
  • On the other hand, …
  • To sum up, … Thank you — are there any questions?
